extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys, government lawyers, judges and clerks dealing with FOIA reverse-disclosure litigation (government contractors and OFCCP practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: A Supreme Court petition and supporting brief addressing (1) whether FOIA Exemption 4 mandates nondisclosure of private commercial information, (2) whether agency regulations under 5 U.S.C. §301 can constitute 'authorization by law' under 18 U.S.C. §1905, and (3) the proper scope of judicial review in suits to enjoin disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA Exemption 4 — scope and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemption 4 of the Freedom of Information Act protects 'trade secrets and commercial or financial information obtained from a person and privileged or confidential' (5 U.S.C. §552(b)(4)). The petition argues that Exemption 4 mandates that private, confidential commercial information which falls within that exemption not be publicly disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history indicates Exemption 4 was intended to protect confidentiality of private business information; some circuits (e.g., Fourth Circuit in Westinghouse) treat Exemption 4 as conferring a right to prevent disclosure, while others (Third, D.C., Fifth Circuits) have held agencies retain discretion to disclose even exempt material. The petition urges recognition of a distinction between exemptions protecting agency information and those protecting private information (Exemptions 4 and 6) and argues nondisclosure should be mandatory for private information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to disclose exempt information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Circuit held that FOIA exemptions do not necessarily make nondisclosure mandatory and that agencies have discretion to disclose information that otherwise falls within an exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holding conflicts with other circuits. The brief frames the issue as whether agencies may waive or disregard protections Congress intended to provide private submitters by choosing to disclose under agency rules, and the potential for conflict with criminal liability under 18 U.S.C. §1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. §1905 — prohibition on unauthorized disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1905 makes it unlawful for government officers or employees to 'publish, divulge, disclose, or make known in any manner or to any extent not authorized by law' information that 'concerns or relates to the trade secrets, processes, operations, style of work, or apparatus, or to the identity, confidential statistical data, amount or source of any income, profits, losses, or expenditures' of corporations or other persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §1905 imposes criminal penalties (fine, imprisonment, removal). A key issue is whether disclosures made pursuant to agency regulations promulgated under 5 U.S.C. §301 constitute 'authorization by law' that would render disclosure lawful under §1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether agency regulations under 5 U.S.C. §301 constitute 'authorization by law' for §1905
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether disclosures made pursuant to agency regulations promulgated under 5 U.S.C. §301 are 'authorized by law' within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. §1905. The Third Circuit held they are; the D.C. Circuit (Charles River Park) held they are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution requires interpreting §301's scope and the 1958 amendment's legislative history. The petition argues allowing agencies to immunize disclosure by internal regulation would permit the executive to define criminal liability for itself and is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review in reverse FOIA suits (de novo vs. APA review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person seeking to enjoin governmental disclosure of information (on grounds Exemption 4 or §1905 applies) is entitled to a trial de novo in district court, or whether review is limited to APA-style review (arbitrary, capricious, abuse of discretion) of the agency record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FOIA §552(a)(4)(B) provides for de novo determination when a court enjoins an agency from withholding records and places burden on the agency; the Third Circuit held review is under the APA unless agency factfinding is inadequate. The petition urges that submitters deserve de novo review (including in camera review) to protect private rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA procedural requisites for requests and judicial action
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency must make records available upon request that reasonably describes the records and is made in accordance with published rules (5 U.S.C. §552(a)(3)). On complaint the district court has jurisdiction to enjoin the agency and 'shall determine the matter de novo' and may examine records in camera, with the burden on the agency to sustain withholding (5 U.S.C. §552(a)(4)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural rules govern where actions may be brought (venues listed) and the standard/process for judicial review in disclosure disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption 3 — statutes exempting disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemption 3 covers information 'specifically exempted from disclosure by statute ... provided that such statute (A) requires that the matters be withheld from the public in such a manner as to leave no discretion on the issue, or (B) establishes particular criteria for withholding or refers to particular types of matters to be withheld.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A related threshold question in reverse FOIA litigation is whether §1905 itself is an Exemption 3 statute (conflicting circuit authority exists). If §1905 qualifies, documents whose disclosure would violate §1905 may be exempt under FOIA Exemption 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFCCP disclosure standard — public interest and agency function test (41 C.F.R. §60‑40.2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: OFCCP regulation: 'records shall be made available for inspection and copying... if it is determined that the requested inspection and copying furthers the public interest and does not impede any of the functions of the OFCC[P] or the Compliance Agencies except in the case of records disclosure of which is prohibited by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulation conditions disclosure on a public-interest showing and on avoiding impediment to OFCCP functions; it also recognizes statutory prohibitions as absolute bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFCCP rule — affirmative action plans presumptively disclosable (41 C.F.R. §60‑40.2(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmative action plans submitted by contractors 'shall be disclosed' subject to limited exceptions specified in §60‑40.3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although AAPs are generally disclosable under OFCCP policy, §60‑40.3 enumerates particular portions and conditions under which portions may be withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding AAP goals/timetables when indicating major personnel shifts (§60‑40.3(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of affirmative action plans such as goals and timetables that would be 'confidential commercial or financial information because they indicate, and only to the extent that they indicate, that a contractor plans major shifts or changes in his personnel requirements and he has not made this information available to the public' may be withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency should withhold such information only after receiving verification and a satisfactory explanation from the contractor that the information should be withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding staffing patterns and pay scales when release would injure business (§60‑40.3(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of AAPs constituting information on staffing patterns and pay scales may be withheld 'but only to the extent that their release would injure the business or financial position of the contractor, would constitute a release of confidential financial information of an employee or would constitute an unwarranted invasion of the privacy of an employee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fact-intensive determination tied to a showing of injury or privacy concerns; verification from contractor and case-by-case analysis may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other specific OFCCP non‑disclosure categories (§60‑40.3(a)(3)–(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation lists additional categories that are exempt from compulsory disclosure or may be withheld: (3) names of individual complainants; (4) assignments to particular contractors of named compliance officers if disclosure would subject them to harassment or affect enforcement; (5) compliance investigation files including standard compliance review report and related documents during the course of the review or while enforcement action is in progress or contemplated; (6) copies of preemployment selection tests used by contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compliance investigation files, withholding applies only to the extent information constitutes trade secrets/confidential commercial or financial information, inter-/intra-agency memoranda not available in private litigation, personnel/medical files, informant-privilege data, or information whose disclosure is prohibited by statute. Other records may be withheld on a case-by-case basis with Director, OFCC approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: EEO‑1 (Standard Form 100) disclosure status (§60‑40.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Standard Form 100 (EEO‑1) submitted by contractors 'shall be disclosed' pending further instructions from the Director, OFCC; the statutory prohibition in Section 709(e) of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is limited to EEOC personnel and title VII authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OFCCP treated EEO‑1 disclosure as required pending guidance, subject to statutory limits tied to EEOC authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑disclosure hearing and appeal timelines (41 C.F.R. §60‑60.4(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation provides contractors may identify non-disclosable information at submission or when an FOIA request is received; Contract Compliance Office will determine within 10 days whether material is exempt from disclosure; contractor may appeal to Director of OFCC within 10 days; Director must make final determination within 10 days; Director's decision is a final agency decision reviewable under 5 U.S.C. §701 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These short, mandatory timelines constrain agency processing of confidentiality claims. The regulation also treats certain information as part of investigatory files and exempt during compliance review/enforcement activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating 'substantial competitive injury' — manning tables as example
rubrics_metrics.description: District court found that 'manning tables' are confidential and that release could cause substantial competitive harm by (1) aiding employee raiding, (2) permitting competitors to determine exact use of labor force and revealing technology applied, and (3) allowing competitors to reduce their risk‑taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether commercial information merits withholding under Exemption 4 or §1905, courts look to concrete competitive harms such as those above; expert testimony and factual showing on potential misuse by competitors is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA relief where agency action is 'contrary to law' (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: District court enjoined disclosure pursuant to 5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A) after finding disclosure of certain documents was 'contrary to law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where reversal under Exemption 4/§1905 is sought, plaintiffs may seek relief under the APA where agency disclosure decisions violate applicable law or regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow, document‑specific approach to injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court applied a narrow definition of 'manning tables' and issued a permanent injunction listing specific pages that must not be disclosed, indicating that injunctions should be precise and limited to the parts of records that satisfy confidentiality criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may and do identify particular pages/parts that must be withheld rather than enjoining wholesale disclosure; precise factfinding and page-level analysis is used to tailor relief.
